content.text:
Got the full session log via the remote sessions API. Here's the handoff:

## Session Summary — claude.ai/code session (yesterday evening)

**Task Overview:** You asked the cloud agent the same question that started our session — did PR #1893 break checkpoint pushing for non-origin remotes — and then pushed it further into **design territory**: "Can we still sync to whatever remote the push is going to — while still not leaking into multiple remotes?"

**Current State:** Investigation only, no code written. The cloud agent independently reached the same diagnosis we did here: sole non-origin remote still works (tier 3); the broken shapes are multi-remote repos where the push target isn't the elected remote; stranding is silent (debug log only); reads hardcode origin so explicit `checkpoint_push_remote` was the only end-to-end non-origin path.

**Important Discoveries** (beyond what we covered here):
- It found the mid-PR history: #1893 briefly *had* a tracking tier (`branch.<name>.pushRemote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `branch.<name>.remote` ranked above origin), and Stefan dropped it in `74e239a9` after the `TestAlternates` canary caught it making pushes to other remotes silent no-ops.
- It articulated the design asymmetry crisply: follow-the-push **fails open** (transcripts land on a remote you never chose — irreversible), elected-remote **fails closed** (sync deferred — recoverable). #1893 traded least-surprise for least-damage.
- On your "follow the push without leaking" ask, it laid out three candidates: **sticky first-push election** (push target becomes the persisted elected remote — but silent capture by whichever push comes first is the original sin in smaller doses), **unambiguous-only** (what ships today via the sole-remote tier), and **consent-prompted election** (its recommendation at the time — turn the gated push into a one-time prompt).

**Where it stopped — unanswered question.** The session ended at an `AskUserQuestion` you never answered (it was stuck at the permission prompt). It had settled on sticky election being viable and asked you to pick **the rule for when a push is allowed to capture the election**. The log truncates the options, but the first was: *tracking-gated sticky election — a push elects its target only when that target matches the branch's configured push destination (`branch.pushRemote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `branch.remote`); the election persists per-clone and thereafter beats origin.* The remaining options were variants along the first-push-sticky / consent-prompt / keep-current spectrum.

**Context that changed since that session:** we've now shipped PR #1987 (the gated-push stderr hint), which is the passive cousin of its "consent" option, and the #1956 → #1951 read-side stack removes the "non-origin elections can't be read back" constraint it flagged as the blocker for any auto-election design.

So the question that session was waiting on is now yours to answer, with better context than it had: **do you want to pursue automatic election capture at all — and if so, which capture rule?**

1. **Tracking-gated sticky election** — a push to the branch's configured push destination captures the election, persisted per-clone; safest of the automatic options since git config expresses intent, not accident.
2. **Consent-prompted election** — the gated push asks once ("elect `fork` as your checkpoint remote?") on an interactive terminal; #1987's hint is already the non-TTY fallback.
3. **Stay where we are** — hint (#1987) + explicit `checkpoint_push_remote`, and revisit after the read-side stack merges (that was the deferred product call in #1951's notes anyway).

Which way do you want to take it?
(branch.pushRemote → remote.pushDefault → branch.remote); the election persists per-clone and thereafter beats origin. is this what matches most similar to what was before 1893 shipped?

Not exactly — it's worth being precise about what "before 1893" was, because nothing on that list replicates it and that's deliberate:

**Before #1893 there was no election at all.** Checkpoints rode *every* push to *any* remote — push to origin, they land on origin; push to your fork, they land on the fork too; push to a public mirror, transcripts land there as well. It was fan-out. That's the privacy leak the PR existed to kill, so "match pre-1893 exactly" isn't on the menu — every option keeps the one-destination invariant.

What tracking-gated sticky election matches is the pre-1893 **experience for the common user** — someone who habitually pushes one remote and never thinks about it. For them, pre-1893 meant "checkpoints go where my pushes go," and this option restores that: your `git push` (to the remote your branch is configured to push to) captures the election, and checkpoints flow there from then on, no config file. The reporter's repos would have kept working with zero setup.

Where it differs from pre-1893 — all deliberately:
- **One destination, ever.** The occasional `git push upstream` or push to a mirror carries nothing. Pre-1893 it would have sprayed transcripts there.
- **Capture requires configured intent, not accident.** Only a push matching `branch.pushRemote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `branch.remote` can elect — git config the user (or their clone setup) put there, not just whichever push happened first.
- **It persists.** Once captured, that remote beats origin from then on, even for reads (after the #1956/#1951 stack).

It's also worth knowing this is essentially the resurrection of the tracking **tier** that Stefan dropped from #1893 pre-merge (`74e239a9`) — with two fixes for why it was dropped: the dropped tier elected the tracking remote *statically*, which turned pushes to any other remote (including origin, in the `clone -o base` topology) into silent no-ops even when you'd never pushed the tracking remote at all; sticky capture only fires on an actual push to that target. And the "can't be read back" half of the objection dissolves once the read-side stack merges.

So: closest in spirit to pre-1893 for the single-push-remote workflow, but it's really "the dropped tracking tier, done safely" rather than a return to follow-the-push.
what is the dropped tracking tier then

It was an election tier that lived inside PR #1893 for a few days mid-review and was deleted before merge (commit `74e239a9`, Stefan, Aug 7). Concretely, the precedence during that window was:

1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` (explicit config)
2. **the branch's configured push destination** — read from git config as `branch.<name>.pushRemote`, else `remote.pushDefault`, else `branch.<name>.remote` ← *the tracking tier*
3. `origin`, if it exists
4. sole remote
5. first in `.git/config` order

The idea was exactly the instinct you've been circling: most people's branches already *say* where they push (that's what `git push` with no arguments uses), so elect that instead of blindly preferring origin. A fork user whose branch tracks `myfork` would get checkpoints on `myfork` with zero config.

**Why it was dropped** — the failure mode is subtle and comes from how the gate works. The tier read git config *statically* at election time; it didn't care where you were actually pushing. And the gate compares the elected name against the remote of the push being made. Combine those and you get: if your branch tracks remote A but you push remote B, the push is gated — *including when B is origin*. The concrete regression that caught it: `TestAlternates_RelativeObjectAlternate_CheckpointSync` does `git clone -o base` (so `branch.remote` is `base`) and then adds and pushes a separate `origin` — the tracking tier elected `base`, so every push to `origin` became a silent no-op and checkpoints never left the machine. Anyone with `remote.pushDefault` set globally, or a `-o`-named clone, hit the same thing. The second objection was that read paths (resume/explain) hardcoded origin, so a tracking-elected non-origin remote produced checkpoints that couldn't be read back from the same clone.

**The difference from the sticky option on the table now:** the tier was a *passive config read* — your git config alone decided the destination, whether or not you ever pushed there, which is what made pushes elsewhere silently dead. Sticky capture inverts that: nothing changes until you *actually push* the remote your branch is configured for; that real event captures the election and persists it. The `clone -o base` case then behaves correctly — if you only ever push origin, origin just stays elected (or gets captured), because `base` never receives a push. And the read-back objection is what the #1956 → #1951 stack removes.

So: same intent as the dropped tier (checkpoints follow your configured push habit), but triggered by demonstrated behavior instead of inferred from config at rest — which is precisely what kills the silent-no-op topology that got the tier deleted.
it didn't care where you were actually pushing. - well this is wrong obviously right

Right — and here's the sharp part: that flaw isn't unique to the dropped tier. It's the same structural defect the **origin tier has today**, just pointed at different victims.

Any election rule that picks a destination from config *at rest* — without reference to where pushes actually go — can elect a remote you never push. When that happens, the gate makes every real push a no-op and checkpoints strand. The tracking tier did it to people with stray tracking config (`clone -o base`, a global `remote.pushDefault`) who actually push origin. The origin tier does it to people with a dormant origin who actually push somewhere else — which is *exactly* the reporter's bug. #1893 didn't eliminate the defect by dropping the tracking tier; it swapped which population gets hit, betting (reasonably) that "actually pushes origin" is the much bigger population.

That's why the sticky-capture idea is the principled fix rather than another re-aim: it's the only design on the table where the elected remote is, by construction, a remote you demonstrably push — election grounded in observed behavior instead of inferred from config. The tracking-*gated* part then just narrows which observed push is allowed to capture (only your branch's configured destination, so a one-off `git push mirror` can't grab the election by accident).

And #1987's hint is the complement for the residual gap that no election rule can close: whenever the elected remote and the push target disagree, at least it's no longer silent.

If you want to take the sticky design forward, the next concrete step would be writing it up against the open questions the cloud session never got to: what happens to an existing election when tracking config changes, whether origin-elected-by-default counts as "captured" or stays overridable, and where the persisted election lives (it's per-clone state, so presumably `.git/` or `settings.local.json`). Want me to draft that as a Linear issue / design note, or leave it as a product call for the team thread first?
without reference to where pushes actually go — can elect a remote you never push - then why wouldn't we chose where we're pushing then?

Because "where you're pushing" isn't one place — and the moment it's two places, choosing the push target *is* the leak.

If the election just follows each push, then over a week you push `work` (checkpoints land there), then `git push upstream feature-x` for a PR (transcripts land on upstream), then a mirror (transcripts land there too). That's not an election anymore — it's pre-1893 fan-out, arriving one push at a time. The whole point of #1893 is that the set of remotes you push *code* to is routinely broader than the set of places your *session transcripts* should live, and a transcript on the wrong remote is unrecoverable in a way a delayed sync isn't.

So "choose where we're pushing" has to answer: **which push?** That's the entire design question, and it's why the cloud session called the pure form logically impossible and landed on sticky capture:

- **Every push** → fan-out, the privacy leak, rejected.
- **The first push** → one destination, but captured by whichever push happens first — often exactly the wrong one (the upstream you're PRing against), silently and permanently.
- **The push that matches your branch's configured push destination** → this *is* "choose where we're pushing," just with a filter that distinguishes your habitual push remote from a one-off. Your everyday `git push` captures the election; a stray `git push upstream` can't.

So the tracking-gated sticky option isn't an alternative to "elect where we push" — it's the version of it that survives the multi-remote case. The tracking config isn't the *source* of the election (that was the dropped tier's mistake); it's just the *guard* that says which real push counts as "where I push" versus "somewhere I pushed once."

The one scenario it leaves imperfect: someone whose branch has no tracking config and who pushes explicitly (`git push gh main` every time). Their pushes never match a configured destination, so nothing captures and they fall back to today's tiers + the #1987 hint. That's the residual you'd be accepting.
so what do we do abotu this then What was the issue with using the same remote as the push? (that doesn't appear in the logic sequence at all).  Going by principle of least surprise, I'm surprised

Here's the answer to that objection, and the plan I'd put behind it:

**The honest answer to "why isn't the push target in the sequence":** it was left out on purpose, because "sync to the remote being pushed" *was* the old behavior, and it's the thing #1893 was killing — in a multi-remote repo it means every remote you ever push code to eventually receives your session transcripts. The two failure modes aren't symmetric: follow-the-push fails **open** (transcripts on a remote you never chose — irreversible), elected-remote fails **closed** (sync deferred — recoverable). So least-surprise was deliberately traded for least-damage. That trade is defensible; what wasn't defensible is that the surprising half was *silent* — you found out by noticing checkpoints missing.

**What we do about it — three steps, two already in motion:**

1. **Kill the silence (done, PR #1987):** a gated push now tells you checkpoints are waiting, where they're headed, and what to set. The surprise still exists but announces itself with the fix attached.
2. **Unblock non-origin elections (in flight, #1956 → #1951):** reads currently hardcode origin, which was half the reason the push-target idea was rejected — an auto-elected non-origin remote produced checkpoints that couldn't be read back. That objection dissolves when the stack merges.
3. **Restore follow-the-push in its safe form (the new work):** tracking-gated sticky election — a push captures the election when its target matches the branch's configured push destination, persisted per-clone, one destination ever. That gives the "checkpoints go where my pushes go" experience back for exactly the reporter's case, without per-push fan-out and without the dropped tier's config-at-rest bug. It slots between tiers 1 and 2 and needs a short design note (capture semantics when tracking config changes, where the per-clone election lives).

If you want to reply in the thread, something like:

> It was on purpose — "sync wherever the push goes" was the old behavior, and in multi-remote repos it meant session transcripts landed on every remote you pushed code to, which is worse than a deferred sync (one's irreversible). But agreed the silent version of that trade was wrong: [#1987] makes the push say so, and once the read-side work lands we want election to follow your actual push habit (sticky, one destination) instead of preferring a dormant origin.

Want me to file the step-3 design as a Linear issue so it's on the record as the follow-up?

tracking-gated sticky election — a push captures the election when its target matches the branch's configured push destination, - does this match/cover what we talked about earlier which was with forks/mirrors

Yes — it covers each scenario we walked through, and the way it lands on each one is worth checking explicitly, because the fork and mirror cases are supposed to come out *differently*:

**The fork workflow (origin = unpushable upstream, you push your fork):** covered, and this is the case the design exists for. In practice a fork user's branch tracks the fork (`git push -u fork feature` sets it; so does `remote.pushDefault=fork`). Their normal push matches the configured destination → captures the election → checkpoints flow to the fork from then on, beating the dormant origin. This was previously the "set `checkpoint_push_remote` by hand" case — sticky capture automates exactly it. The reporter's repos are this shape or its cousin (renamed remote), so they'd have kept working with zero config.

**The mirror case:** covered in the *other* direction — a one-off `git push mirror branch` does **not** match the branch's configured push destination, so it captures nothing and carries nothing. That's the privacy property surviving: transcripts don't land on the mirror, the election doesn't flip to it, and the #1987 hint fires so it isn't silent. The only way a mirror ever receives checkpoints is if it literally *is* your configured push destination — at which point it isn't "a mirror" in the relevant sense, it's where you work.

**The `clone -o base` topology (the one that killed the dropped tier):** covered. Your branch tracks `base`, but you only ever push the separately-added `origin` — those pushes don't match `base`, so no capture happens, tiers fall through to origin (tier 2), pushes sync. The dropped tier broke here precisely because it elected `base` from config without any push; sticky capture can't, because `base` never sees a push.

## 1. Persisted election state (new)

Per-clone, shared across worktrees → lives in the git **common dir** (alongside the push queue's precedent), e.g. `.git/entire/checkpoint-sync-remote.json`: `{remote, captured_at, capture_reason}`. ## 2. Resolver: one new tier + one new source

`sessions-and-checkpoints.md` election section, CLAUDE.md strategy bullet, prominent changelog entry ("checkpoints follow the remote your branches push, captured on first push").

can you be explicit in what capture is really doing

Capture is one narrow thing: **the pre-push hook writing down a remote name the first time it sees you push to the place your branch is configured to push.** Everything else in the system stays as it is. Explicitly:

**What exists today (after #1893):** every time the pre-push hook runs, it computes "the elected remote" from scratch — config setting, else origin, else sole remote, else first in `.git/config` — and compares it to the remote you're pushing. Match → checkpoints ride along. No match → nothing happens. The election is *stateless*: it's re-derived per push from config that says nothing about your actual behavior.

**What capture adds — mechanically, step by step.** During a `git push fork feature-x`, before the gate runs:

1. The hook asks git: "for the branch being pushed, where is it *configured* to push?" — `branch.feature-x.pushRemote`, else `remote.pushDefault`, else `branch.feature-x.remote`. Say the answer is `fork`.
2. It compares that to the push target. Pushing `fork`, configured for `fork` → match. (Pushing `mirror` while configured for `fork` → no match, capture does nothing, today's behavior exactly.)
3. On a match — and only if you haven't set `checkpoint_push_remote`, and `fork` isn't already the elected remote — it **writes one small file** in `.git/` recording `{"remote": "fork"}`, and prints one line telling you it did: checkpoints will now sync to `fork`.
4. That's the entire event. It happens at most once per "habit change" — subsequent pushes to `fork` match an election that's already `fork`, so nothing fires.

**What that file then does:** the election resolver gains one tier that reads it. New precedence: your explicit config setting → **the captured remote, if it still exists** → origin → sole → first. So from that push onward, the stateless computation returns `fork`, the gate passes on your `fork` pushes, and checkpoints flow there — including the very push that did the capturing.

**What capture is *not*:**
- It's not "sync to whatever I'm pushing" — a push to any remote that *isn't* your branch's configured destination changes nothing and carries nothing.
- It's not a new sync mechanism — the gate, the push code, the queue, the privacy properties are untouched. Capture only changes the answer to "which one remote?"
- It's not config inference at rest — nothing is decided by reading git config alone (the dropped tier's bug). The trigger is an actual push event that *agrees* with the config.

**So the whole feature is:** one JSON file in `.git/`, one write site in the pre-push hook guarded by "push target == branch's configured push destination," one read tier in the resolver, one stderr line announcing the change. In plain words: *the first time you push where your branch says you push, Entire remembers that remote as your checkpoint home.*

**Signal 1: you actually pushed there.** Rules out everything config-only — the dropped tier's bug, the `clone -o base` ghost, a `remote.pushDefault` you set globally and forgot. A remote that never receives a push can never be elected by capture.

**Signal 2: git config *declares* that remote as this branch's push destination.** This is the one doing the anti-upstream work, so let me be exact about the one-off PR push. Fork workflow: you cloned your fork or did `git push -u fork feature-x`, so `branch.feature-x.remote` is `fork`. Now you contribute upstream: `git push upstream feature-x`. Capture asks "where is `feature-x` configured to push?" — answer `fork`. Push target `upstream` ≠ `fork` → **no capture, no checkpoints, nothing**. The key property: a one-off push is, almost by definition, an *explicit-name* push to somewhere your branch doesn't track — so it structurally can't satisfy signal 2. Say you're a contributor with push rights whose branches actually track `upstream` and who pushes there routinely. Capture elects upstream, transcripts go to upstream. Is that wrong? That last point is the practical answer: single-election capture is the set design with max-size 1, so building capture first isn't a competing bet — it's phase one, and lifting the cap is phase two (queue rework + plural config). If that matches what you meant, the scope I gave earlier stands with one amendment — the persisted state file should be shaped as a list from day one (`{"remotes": ["fork"]}`) so lifting the cap never needs a migration.

It's exactly as automatic as capture — because it *is* capture, just writing into a list instead of overwriting a single slot. "Consented" doesn't mean "configured"; consent comes from the same two-signal evidence, per remote:

**What happens with zero config, lifecycle of a typical repo:**

1. **Seeding:** today's tiers pick the initial member (origin, or the sole remote, or first-in-config). Out of the box, behavior is identical to now.
2. **First push to your fork** (branch tracks it): evidence rule fires → `fork` joins the set, one stderr line announces it, that same push carries the checkpoints. No file touched by the user.
3. **You also routinely push a `work` remote from branches that track it:** same thing — `work` joins on its first tracking-matched push. Now both of "your" remotes carry checkpoints, which is the exact outcome you were asking for, and nobody opened an editor.
4. **One-off `git push upstream`** for a PR: no tracking match → never joins, never receives anything, hint fires if checkpoints are waiting elsewhere.

**Where a human is genuinely irreplaceable — and it's veto, not setup:**

- The remote you *do* track and push but don't want transcripts on (the contributor-with-upstream-push-rights case). No signal distinguishes it from your fork; only you know. That's what the announcement is for — the moment it auto-joins, you're told, and the fix is one line (an exclusion or a `checkpoint_push_remote`-style pin). Config as **override**, never as prerequisite.
- **Removal** when your habits change — auto-evicting a remote you've merely stopped pushing lately is too clever (vacation ≠ revocation), so leaving the set is manual. Cheap and rare.

So the config surface doesn't grow for the happy path at all — it's the same "explicit setting always wins" escape hatch that exists today, extended to say "never" as well as "always." The design dial is only *how loud* the automatic join is:

- **Announce-and-proceed** (what I described): fully automatic, opt-out. Right default for the population that's complaining — they want it to just work.
- **Ask-on-join** (the consent prompt): first tracking-matched push to a new remote asks once; non-TTY falls back to the hint. One interruption per remote per clone, ever, and nothing self-elects silently.

Those aren't even mutually exclusive — announce for the seed member (it's just preserving today's behavior), ask for each *additional* member (that's the moment transcripts would start existing in a second place, which is the privacy-relevant event). That split is probably the right product answer: automatic where it's restoring what users expect, one explicit yes where it's genuinely expanding exposure.
so consented is when you push to a remote thats basically you consenting and your checkpoitns will automatically be synced then?

Almost — with one word of precision that carries all the weight: **not any push. A push to the remote your branch is configured to push.**

A bare push can't be consent — that's precisely the pre-#1893 bug. Your one-off `git push upstream feature-x` for a PR is a push, but nobody would say it consents to your session transcripts living on upstream. If pushing alone consented, we've rebuilt the leak.

So the consent event is the **agreement of two things you did**:

1. You configured the branch to push there (`git push -u fork …`, or `remote.pushDefault` — declaration), *and*
2. you actually pushed there (behavior).

Declaration alone was the dropped tier's bug (elects a remote you never push). Behavior alone is the leak (elects a remote you pushed by accident). The intersection is the closest thing to consent that git's existing signals can express — "this is where I told git my work goes, and I did in fact send it there."

Then yes: the moment that fires for a remote, it becomes checkpoint-carrying, and syncing there is automatic from that push onward — with the two guardrails we've discussed doing the honesty work:

- **It's announced** the moment it happens (or, in ask-mode for second-and-later remotes, it's a one-time question instead) — so "consent" is never something the tool inferred in silence; you're told exactly when and where transcripts start flowing, with the veto in the same line.
- **Explicit config outranks it** in both directions — pin one remote, or exclude one — for the cases where the signals genuinely can't know your intent (the upstream you also track and push).

So the one-sentence version of the whole model: *your git configuration nominates remotes, your actual pushes confirm them, Entire tells you when a confirmation happens, and your settings can overrule everything.*
how would it be zero config then with the declaration

Because the declaration isn't config you write for Entire — it's config git already wrote for you as a side effect of your normal workflow. That's the trick of the whole design: it reads intent from state that already exists.

Where `branch.<name>.remote` / `pushRemote` / `pushDefault` actually come from:

- **`git clone`** sets `branch.main.remote = origin` on its own. You've never touched it, it's there.
- **`git push -u fork feature`** — the thing every fork-workflow user runs once per branch so that plain `git push` works afterward — sets `branch.feature.remote = fork` as a side effect. The user was setting up their push shorthand, not configuring anything for us.
- **`git push.autoSetupRemote = true`** (common since git 2.37, lots of people have it on globally) does the `-u` automatically on first push — declaration created with literally zero deliberate action.
- **`checkout -b` off a tracked branch** inherits tracking in common setups.

So for the population that's complaining, the declaration already exists in their `.git/config` right now — put there by git, as part of making `git push` work at all. Capture just reads it back. "Zero config" means **zero Entire config**: no `.entire/settings*` edit, no new command, no prompt to answer in the happy path. The user's total lifetime interaction is: work exactly as they already do, see one line announcing where checkpoints now go.

The residual is the flip side of the same coin: someone who never lets git store a push destination — types `git push gh main` explicitly every time, no `-u`, no `pushDefault` — has made no declaration anywhere, so there's genuinely nothing to read. For them capture never fires and they land on today's behavior: tiers + the #1987 hint, which names the one-line explicit setting. That's the honest floor of the design: it can be zero-*additional*-config for everyone whose git already knows where they push (the overwhelming majority, since bare `git push` requires it), and one-line-config for the minority who've opted out of telling git.

can we have multiple declrations and remotes still i guess from this

Yes — that's exactly what the set design (phase 2) is. To be concrete about what "multiple" looks like in one repo:

**Multiple declarations:** they're per-branch, so this is already natural — `main` declares `origin`, `feature/*` declare `fork`, some release branch declares `work`. Git holds all of these simultaneously; nothing about the design assumes one.

**Multiple confirmed remotes:** each (declared ∧ pushed) pair joins the set independently, whenever its confirming push happens. Three remotes can all be members. Each one earned its place the same way, each join was announced once, and config can evict or pin any of them.

**What syncing means with N members:** a push to member X carries everything X hasn't received yet — to X only. Other members catch up on *their* next push. So members converge on the full checkpoint history at their own pace (a remote you push daily stays current; one you push weekly lags a week), and no push ever touches a remote other than its own target. Nothing fans out — that invariant survives. The engineering that makes this work is the per-remote pending state in the git-refs queue ("which refs has each member received"), which is the one real build item of phase 2; the git-branch backend needs nothing, since a branch push to each remote already tracks per-remote.

**Reads:** union across all members plus origin-legacy — the shape #1956/#1951 already implement, just with a longer candidate list. Any single member is sufficient to recover everything once it's converged.

So the ladder, complete: today (one remote, guessed) → capture (one remote, evidence-chosen, size-1 set) → full set (all your confirmed remotes carry, each converging independently). Same trigger, same state file, same announcement mechanic at every rung — phase 2 only removes the cap and teaches the queue to count per remote.

That's the whole design settled, as far as I can tell: evidence-based membership, no-ping-pong stability in phase 1, list-shaped state from day one, queue rework deferred to phase 2. Shall I start building phase 1?

input.new_string:
Committed checkpoints sync to exactly one git remote — the elected checkpoint
sync remote, resolved in this order:

1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` if set — fail-closed when it
   names a remote that is not configured (checkpoint sync is disabled until
   fixed, since this is explicit user intent).
2. The **captured** election, if its remote is still configured — fail-soft
   otherwise (capture is automatic state, so a renamed/removed remote falls
   through instead of disabling sync).
3. `origin`, if configured.
4. The sole configured remote.
5. The first remote in `.git/config` order.

**Capture** is how the election follows the user's actual push habit with
zero configuration: during pre-push, when the push target agrees with the
branch's declared push destination (`branch.<name>.pushRemote` →
`remote.pushDefault` → `branch.<name>.remote` — the config a bare `git push`
resolves through) and differs from the current election, that remote is
persisted as the captured election (git common dir,
`entire-checkpoint-sync-remotes.json`, list-shaped for the future multi-remote
set), a one-line stderr notice announces the change, and the same push carries
the checkpoints. Declaration alone never elects (the config-at-rest bug that
got the static tracking tier dropped in `74e239a9` — it turned pushes to every

input.content:
## Problem

The single-remote election (ENT-1451, v0.10.0) guesses the checkpoint sync destination from config at rest: `checkpoint_push_remote` -> `origin` -> sole -> first in `.git/config`. A user whose branches push a non-origin remote loses that election to a dormant origin, so every push is gated and checkpoints strand locally until they discover and hand-configure `checkpoint_push_remote`. The first user report landed the day after release ("I have a bunch of repos where the git remote I push to isn't called origin. It looks like this means I no longer push checkpoints.").

#1893 fixed "checkpoints sync where they shouldn't" (transcript fan-out) but left "checkpoints don't sync where they should" as an opt-in config remedy. This PR is the second half.

## Change

**Capture**: during pre-push, a push whose target agrees with the branch's declared push destination (`branch.<name>.pushRemote` -> `remote.pushDefault` -> `branch.<name>.remote` — the config a bare `git push` resolves through) and differs from the current election persists that remote as the **captured election**, announces it on stderr, and the same push carries the checkpoints:

```
[entire] Checkpoints now sync to "fork" — the remote your branch pushes to. Override with strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote in .entire/settings.local.json.
```

New election precedence: explicit setting (fail-closed, unchanged) -> **captured** (fail-soft: a renamed/removed captured remote falls through instead of disabling sync) -> origin -> sole -> first.

**Neither signal elects alone.** Declaration without a push is the config-at-rest bug that got the static tracking tier dropped pre-merge in #1893 (`74e239a9`: a `clone -o base` stranded every origin push — pinned by `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_TrackingAloneDoesNotReroute`); a push without declaration is the pre-#1893 transcript leak (a one-off `git push upstream` for a PR must never publish transcripts). Capture acts only on their intersection.

**Phase-1 rules** (multi-remote set is the follow-up):
- At most one captured remote; **first capture sticks** — a mixed-habit repo whose branches push two remotes cannot flip the election per push.
- State is list-shaped from day one (`.git/entire-checkpoint-sync-remotes.json`, `{"remotes":[...]}`) so lifting the cap needs no migration.
- Explicit `checkpoint_push_remote` outranks and disables capture; dedicated `checkpoint_remote` URL mode and `push_sessions: false` never reach it.
- `entire status` renders the source: `fork (captured from your pushes)`; `--json` reports `checkpoint_sync_remote_source: "captured"`.

## Test changes worth reviewer attention

The existing single-remote integration tests set up their gated remote with `push -u`, which under capture is a *declared* destination — pushing it now legitimately re-elects. Their setups reset tracking (`setBranchTrackingRemote`) so they keep pinning the undeclared-one-off shape, and `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute` is split into its two surviving truths:

- `TrackingAloneDoesNotReroute`: a tracked-but-never-pushed remote still never receives data and captures nothing (the `74e239a9` regression pin).
- `TrackedPushCapturesElection`: the fork topology end to end — capture fires, the same push delivers, origin is gated thereafter, status reports `captured`.

Unit: captured-tier precedence table, capture predicate table (declaration precedence, already-elected no-op, first-capture-sticks, config disable, raw-URL), corrupt/missing state fail-soft.

## Sequencing

**Merge after #1956 -> #1951.** Reads still resolve through origin until that stack lands; merging capture first would route checkpoints to a remote other clones cannot read from. Nothing in this diff depends on the stack's code — the read chain picks up the captured election automatically once both exist.

Not done here, deliberately: multi-remote set (needs per-remote push-queue state — ENT-1494's rescope), capture from pushed refspecs rather than HEAD's branch (hook doesn't plumb stdin refspecs; a miss is conservative), `entire clean` leaving the state file (parity with the push-queue file).

## Testing

`mise run fmt` clean, `mise run lint` 0 issues, full unit suite (8,846), full integration suite (475), Vogon canary — all green.

Phase 1 is built, verified, and up as **draft PR #1991**: https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1991

**What shipped on the branch** (`feat/checkpoint-sync-capture`, own worktree, off latest main):

- **`strategy/checkpoint_sync_capture.go`** — the whole feature: list-shaped state file in the git common dir (`entire-checkpoint-sync-remotes.json`), the capture trigger (push target must agree with the branch's declared push destination: `branch.pushRemote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `branch.remote`), the stderr announcement pointing at `settings.local.json`, and atomic fail-soft persistence.
- **Resolver**: new `captured` tier between the explicit setting and origin — fail-soft (a renamed captured remote falls through instead of disabling sync, unlike the fail-closed explicit setting).
- **`prePush`**: capture runs just before the gate, so the electing push is also the first push that carries the checkpoints.
- **Status**: `Checkpoints sync to: fork (captured from your pushes)`, JSON source `captured`.
- **Docs**: election section rewritten in `sessions-and-checkpoints.md` and CLAUDE.md.

**Tests** (TDD both layers — watched each fail first): 13 new unit subtests covering the tier precedence and every capture guard, plus integration scenarios for the fork topology end-to-end (capture fires, same push delivers, origin gated afterward, status reports `captured`), the `clone -o base` immunity pin, and the undeclared one-off. One design-consequence worth knowing: the existing gate tests set up remotes with `push -u`, which under capture *is* a declaration — so their setups now reset tracking, and `BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute` was split into its two surviving truths (tracking alone never reroutes; tracking + push captures). Full unit (8,846), full integration (475), and the Vogon canary are all green; lint 0 issues.

**Two things to know:**
1. It's a **draft** because of the agreed merge order — after #1956 → #1951, so captured non-origin elections are readable end-to-end. The code has no dependency on the stack; only the merge does.
2. One transient hiccup mid-commit: backticks in my commit message got executed as shell substitution (a stray bare `git push` ran and failed harmlessly on upstream mismatch — nothing was pushed by it). The message was amended clean before the real push.

The full arc is now in flight: #1987 (hint, review-complete) → #1956/#1951 (reads follow election, your open stack) → #1991 (capture, draft) — with phase 2 (the consented multi-remote set, per-remote queue state) scoped in the PR body as the ENT-1494 rescope.
